title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & benchmarking playbook
author: Marcus Chen
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling guidance, profiling playbooks, the canonical benchmarking suite, recent release notes, known issues, incident runbooks, and team wiki links. It is intended as the single source of truth for engineers operating and evolving Redwood's inference runtime.

Owners & contacts
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime team (on-call rotation: runtime-oncall@redwood.example.com)
- Runtime lead: Marcus Chen
- Performance lead: Aisha Patel
- SRE escalation: Liam O'Connor

Service overview
- Services in scope: request-router, batcher, kernel-scheduler, executor, kv-cache, metrics-agent, trace-collector
- Primary goals: predictable latency (SLOs), high throughput, deterministic fallbacks, cost-efficient batching/caching

SLOs & operational targets
- P95 latency (generation <=512 tokens): <= 120ms
- P99 latency (generation <=512 tokens): <= 250ms
- Availability (platform inference endpoints): 99.95% monthly
- Error budget: 0.05% per month
- Cost target: average tokens-per-second per-GPU cost below monthly benchmark for each instance class (see Benchmark table)

Runtime architecture (high level)
1) Request router
   - Handles authentication, rate limiting, routing policy (latency/cost/region).
   - Outputs a plan: model variant, target pool, max-acceptable-latency.
2) Batcher
   - Continuous batching with dynamic target batch size (based on request arrival curve and target latency).
   - Supports priority lanes for low-latency traffic.
3) Kernel scheduler (core of this doc)
   - Matches requested op graphs to optimized kernels and execution plan.
   - Chooses: precision (fp16/int8), kernel implementation (fused-attention / flash-attn / custom GEMM), pipelined vs fused execution, memory placement.
4) KV cache manager
   - Shared per-session prefix caching, ECC-aware eviction policy, per-customer residency controls.
5) Executor & hardware runtime
   - Inference engine running on GPUs (NVIDIA A100/H100, AMD MI250 as deployed). Uses per-architecture kernel sets and device-specific heuristics.

Kernel scheduling: policies & heuristics
- Objective: minimize p99 latency while maximizing average GPU utilization and respecting memory headroom.
- Heuristics order: 1) compatibility check (model-arch vs kernel), 2) latency budget check, 3) batch size optimization, 4) kernel cost model evaluation, 5) choice of quantization/precision.
- Kernel selection rules:
  - Small sequences (<=128 tokens): prefer low-overhead kernels optimized for small batch sizes (e.g., fused-kernel-v2).
  - Medium sequences (129-512): prefer batched GEMM with flash-attention if available.
  - Long sequences (>512): prefer chunked attention kernels with streaming KV cache to reduce peak memory.
  - For multi-GPU pipeline: prefer compute-balanced partitioning minimizing inter-device NVLink transfers.
- Quantization decision tree:
  - If model supports int8 and workload is throughput-first (no strict quality SLO), use int8-quantized kernels.
  - If generation quality is critical (regressions flagged by evals), use fp16 kernels.
- Kernel fallback sequence: primary -> compatibility fallback -> lower-performance kernel -> model-variant fallback. Fallbacks must be logged with reason and latency delta predicted.

Profiling playbook (when to run and how)
Purpose: collect reproducible traces to diagnose p99/throughput regressions and kernel behavior.

Step 0: Preconditions- Only run on staging or isolated capacity. Notify on-call and perf lead.

Step 1: Reproduce workload- Use the canonical benchmarking harness to replay real requests (see Benchmarking section). Use recorded user traffic where permitted and scrubbed.

Step 2: Lightweight tracing (5-10 minutes)- Enable sampling traces at 1:1000 and collect: request timings, batch-size distribution, kernel decisions.
  - CLI: curl -X POST https://staging-router/_admin/trace -d '{"sample_rate":0.001}'

Step 3: Full profiler (single node)
- Tools: NVIDIA nsys/nsight, ncu, CUPTI counters, rocprof for AMD, Linux perf for host context switches.
- Commands (example, NVIDIA):
  - nsys profile -o run.nsys --capture-range=nvtx --trace=cuda,nvtx -- python3 tools/bench.py --workload chat-short --duration 300
  - ncu --target-processes all --set full --export run.ncu python3 tools/bench.py --workload chat-short --duration 180
- Collect: kernel launch times, SM utilization, memory bandwidth, PCIe/NVLink traffic, kernel occupancy, API overhead.

Step 4: Microbench kernels
- Run the kernel-level microbench harness to measure latency vs batch size and sequence length for each kernel variant.
  - Example: python3 tools/microbench.py --kernel fused-attn --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8,16 --seq-lens 16,64,128,256 --reps 200

Step 5: Interpret results
- Key signposts: high CUDA API overhead (many small kernels), low SM utilization with large memory stalls, NVLink/PCIe bottleneck when sharding state, disproportionate time in memcpy vs compute.

Step 6: Mitigation runbook
1) If high API overhead: fuse kernels or increase batch size for low-priority lanes; enable batched-kernel-path for seq<=128.
2) If memory-bound: prefer chunked attention, reduce kv-cache retention TTL or increase GPU memory class (move to H100).
3) If NVLink saturation: rebalance pipeline, reduce model-parallel sync frequency, or route requests to local-model variants.
4) If quantization quality regression: rollback int8 rollout, capture evaluation dataset and file an issue in model-onboarding.

Benchmarking suite (canonical workloads)
Workloads (canonical labels):
- chat-short: avg tokens/request 60, seq cap 256, p95 target low-latency
- chat-long: avg tokens/request 350, seq cap 2048, throughput-focused
- embeddings: CPU/GPU mixed optimized path, batch sizes up to 256
- throughput-burst: synthetic constant arrival to measure tokens/sec sustained

Benchmark config example (YAML):

benchmark_suite: run-default
- name: chat-short
  concurrency: [1,5,10]
  duration_sec: 300
  seq_len_distribution: "short-heavy"
  model_variants: ["redwood-1.7-fp16","redwood-1.7-int8"]

Hardware matrix (example table):
- GPU class: A100-80GB | H100-80GB | MI250
- Target batch sizes: tuned per GPU, see microbench outputs
- Quantization: fp16 default, int8 optional on throughput lanes

CLI example to run suite:
- python3 tools/bench.py --suite run-default --out results/$(date +%F)-run.json
- analyze: python3 tools/bench_analyze.py --input results/2026-04-05-run.json --report out/report.html

Benchmark acceptance criteria
- Regression guard: no more than 5% p95 increase and 10% p99 increase vs baseline for the same hardware and model variant.
- Cost guard: tokens/sec per GPU must not degrade by >7% vs baseline.

Release notes (recent stable release)
- Release: runtime v1.8.2 (2026-03-25)
  - Improvements: new fused-kernel-v2 for small-sequence paths reducing p95 by ~20% on A100; improved batcher queuing reducing p99 for chat-short by 15%.
  - Kernel scheduler: added explicit cost model for int8 vs fp16 selection and memory-aware scheduling for long-context models.
  - Fixes: corrected KV cache expiry bug that caused cache thrashing under bursty traffic.
  - Known impact: int8 rollout enabled only in throughput pools; manual rollout required for low-latency customer pools.

Known issues (triaged & tracked)
1) Issue: Intermittent p99 spikes for chat-short on H100 when mixed fp16/int8 kernels are co-located.
   - Symptom: p99 spikes by 2-3x for 3-5 minute windows.
   - Workaround: pin workload to homogeneous pools or disable int8 co-location.
   - Owner: runtime-perf (Aisha Patel)
2) Issue: Microburst evictions in KV cache under extreme burst traffic.
   - Symptom: session histories missing causing context truncation.
   - Workaround: temporarily increase kv-cache TTL and enable reserve memory for burst lanes.
   - Owner: runtime-storage (Liam O'Connor)
3) Issue: Rare CUDA driver OOM on node with older drivers when running mixed model-parallel variants.
   - Symptom: node crashes with kernel driver OOM and restarts.
   - Workaround: upgrade to driver >= 535.xx or force single-model GPU packing.

Runtime runbooks (incidents)
A) High p99 latency (production)
1) Immediately: open incident channel #incident-runtime and set status to "investigating".
2) Check global router metrics: request queue depth, per-pool batch sizes, recent kernel fallback logs.
3) Identify whether fault is traffic pattern (spike) or kernel/regression:
   - If traffic spike: throttle non-critical routes, scale Dedicated pools, enable burst capacity.
   - If kernel/regression: binary search model-variant rollouts (rollback int8 flags), pin to last-known-good kernel via runtime flags.
4) Collect traces (sampling 1:100), escalate to perf lead, run microbench on affected node.
5) Post-incident: run full benchmark suite and file a postmortem.

B) Node OOM / GPU driver crash
1) Mark node as unschedulable in capacity pool.
2) Collect diagnostics: dmesg, /var/log/nvidia-installer.log, core dumps.
3) Reboot node if necessary, ensure driver version >= recommended, repro on staging.
4) Restore traffic gradually and monitor p99.

Team wiki & resources
- eng-serving-runtime team wiki: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki (living notes, onboarding)
- Performance dashboards: Grafana -> cluster/runtime-perf (P95/P99 per-model, batch distribution)
- Trace UI: Jaeger -> runtime-traces

Onboarding checklist for new contributors
1) Read this document and the runtime architecture reference.
2) Run the microbench tool against a dev box.
3) Shadow a perf run with an experienced engineer.
4) Be added to oncall rotation after completing runbook drills.

Appendix: quick reference commands
- Start lightweight trace: curl -X POST https://staging-router/_admin/trace -d '{"sample_rate":0.001}'
- Run canonical benchmark: python3 tools/bench.py --suite run-default --out results/2026-04-run.json
- Run microbench: python3 tools/microbench.py --kernel fused-attn --batch-sizes 1,2,4,8 --seq-lens 16,64,128 --reps 200
